query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an optimized, thin anti‐oxidation coating (e.g., an alumina‐forming coating) to the surface of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will inhibit oxygen ingress and pesting at high temperatures without degrading its excellent room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with demonstrated good room-temperature tensile ductility and high elevated-temperature yield strength, but poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thin, adherent, alumina‐forming protective coating (by methods such as electrospark deposition or pack cementation) on the as-cast alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at around 800 °C for an extended period (e.g., 5 hours), while mechanical performance is tested at room temperature and high temperature (e.g., up to 1000 °C) under similar strain rate conditions as previously reported.
generation.structural_mediator: The coating is designed to form a continuous, dense, and slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) layer that acts as a barrier against oxygen diffusion into the alloy substrate.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to high-temperature air, the protective coating rapidly oxidizes to form a stable alumina scale that prevents further oxygen penetration (thus avoiding pesting) while leaving the bulk microstructure—and consequently the mechanical properties—unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the untreated equiatomic alloy which undergoes rapid oxidation and pesting, the coated alloy will exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (minimal scale spallation or degradation) while retaining its original room-temperature ductility (8–16% tensile elongation) and high-temperature yield strength (in the range of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits inadequate oxygen resistance (subject to pesting in air at 800 °C) despite beneficial mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective as long as the coating remains intact under the tested thermal exposure (up to 800 °C for ~5 h in air) and under mechanical loads similar to those evaluated in the baseline studies; extreme thermomechanical cycling or environments outside these limits may affect performance.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adhesion and stability of the coating under cyclic or prolonged thermal exposure, and any subtle impact on fatigue or other dynamic mechanical properties, remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one group with the applied alumina-forming anti-oxidation coating and one control group without any coating. Expose both groups to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, conduct mechanical tests (tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperature) and microstructural/oxidation analyses.
measurements: Thickness and integrity of oxide scales (using SEM and XRD) on both coated and uncoated samples
Quantitative assessment of weight gain due to oxidation
Room temperature tensile ductility and strength
High-temperature yield strength at 1000 °C under comparable strain rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not exhibit a significantly lower degree of oxidation (i.e., similar or excessive oxide degradation or pesting compared to uncoated samples) or if the mechanical properties (tensile ductility and yield strength) are degraded relative to the uncoated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

HfNbTaTiZr is a high-entropy alloy, and according to a calculated VEC value of 4.4, it has a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure. The alloy was developed by mechanical alloying from high-purity metallic powders in a Pulverisette 6 classic line planetary ball mill (Fritsch®, Idar-Oberstein, Germany) with a stainless steel vial and grinding media. Due to the powder reactivity, handling and alloying were performed under an argon atmosphere. To avoid the welding of the alloy to the vial and balls and to reduce the oxidation and contamination of powders, n-heptane was used as a control process agent (PCA). Milling parameters were selected after multiple trials to ensure that the powders were not overheating. A mixture of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr high-purity powders was milled for 60 h, and samples were taken at different time intervals to evaluate the alloying degree. After the alloying process, the particle size was reduced, and a good homogeneity was obtained. With further processing represented by sintering and deposition, the alloying degree was increased.
